topics.label: AuthN vs AuthZ
topics.desc: The core distinction between authentication (proving who you are) and authorization (deciding what you may do), which web frameworks deliberately keep as separate layers.

topics.label: Password-Based Auth
topics.desc: The classic username-and-password login flow, requiring server-side hashing, secure comparison, and lockout policies rather than ever storing or logging the raw credential.

topics.label: Passwordless & Magic Links
topics.desc: Login by emailing a one-time signed link or code (as in Slack or Notion) so users authenticate via control of their inbox instead of a memorized secret.

topics.label: Multi-Factor Auth
topics.desc: Requiring two or more independent factors (something you know, have, or are) so a leaked password alone cannot grant access, the single biggest account-takeover defense.

topics.label: TOTP & Authenticator Apps
topics.desc: Time-based one-time codes (RFC 6238) shown by apps like Google Authenticator or Authy, derived from a shared secret and the current 30-second time window.

topics.label: WebAuthn & Passkeys
topics.desc: The FIDO2/WebAuthn standard using device-bound public-key credentials (passkeys, Touch ID, YubiKeys) for phishing-resistant biometric or hardware login.

topics.label: Account Recovery
topics.desc: Secure password-reset and lost-MFA flows using expiring single-use tokens and backup codes, a frequent weak link that attackers target to bypass strong login.

topics.label: Session-Based Auth
topics.desc: Stateful login where the server stores a session and hands the browser an opaque session ID in a cookie, the default model in frameworks like Django and Rails.

topics.label: Cookie Security Flags
topics.desc: Hardening auth cookies with HttpOnly (no JS access), Secure (HTTPS only), and SameSite (cross-site send rules) to blunt XSS theft and CSRF.

topics.label: Token-Based Auth
topics.desc: Stateless login where the client holds a signed token sent on each request (often as a Bearer header), enabling APIs and SPAs to authenticate without server session state.

topics.label: JWT Structure & Claims
topics.desc: JSON Web Tokens: a base64url header.payload.signature carrying signed claims like sub, exp, and iss, verified without a database lookup but readable by anyone.

topics.label: JWT Signing & Verification
topics.desc: Protecting JWT integrity with HMAC (HS256) or asymmetric (RS256) signatures, while pinning the alg and rejecting the none algorithm to avoid forgery attacks.

topics.label: Access vs Refresh Tokens
topics.desc: Pairing a short-lived access token with a long-lived refresh token so compromised access tokens expire fast while users stay logged in without re-entering credentials.

topics.label: Token Storage & Revocation
topics.desc: Deciding where browsers keep tokens (HttpOnly cookie vs localStorage) and how to revoke them via blocklists or rotation, since stateless JWTs cannot be un-issued.

topics.label: OAuth 2.0
topics.desc: The delegated-authorization framework (RFC 6749) letting an app obtain scoped access tokens to act on a user's behalf without ever seeing their password.

topics.label: OAuth Grant Flows
topics.desc: The flow variants—authorization code (with the PKCE secret for public clients), client credentials, and device code—each chosen to match a client like an SPA, server, or smart TV.

topics.label: OpenID Connect
topics.desc: The identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 adding a signed ID token (JWT) about the user, the modern standard powering Sign in with Google and similar logins.

topics.label: Single Sign-On
topics.desc: One authentication granting access to many applications, the workplace pattern that centralizes login and offboarding through a shared identity provider.

topics.label: SAML
topics.desc: The older XML-based SSO standard still dominant in enterprise, exchanging signed assertions between an identity provider and service provider for federated login.

topics.label: Social Login
topics.desc: Letting users sign in with existing Google, GitHub, or Apple accounts via OAuth/OIDC, reducing signup friction while offloading credential security to the provider.

topics.label: Identity Providers
topics.desc: Managed auth platforms—Auth0, Okta, Clerk, Firebase Auth, and libraries like Auth.js/NextAuth—that implement login, MFA, and SSO so teams avoid rolling their own.

topics.label: RBAC
topics.desc: Role-Based Access Control grouping permissions into roles like admin or editor that are assigned to users, the most common authorization model in business apps.

topics.label: ABAC
topics.desc: Attribute-Based Access Control deciding access from contextual attributes (user dept, resource owner, time, location) for fine-grained rules beyond fixed roles.

topics.label: Permissions, Policies & ACLs
topics.desc: The concrete checks granting specific actions on resources—from per-resource access control lists to centralized policy engines like Open Policy Agent, Oso, or Casbin.

topics.label: Least Privilege
topics.desc: Granting every user, service, and token only the minimum permissions its job requires, shrinking the blast radius when any single credential is compromised.

topics.label: Multi-Tenancy Isolation
topics.desc: Scoping every query and resource to its owning tenant so one customer's data can never leak to another in shared-database SaaS, often enforced via row-level security.

topics.label: Object-Level Authorization
topics.desc: Verifying the requester actually owns the specific record before acting, the missing check behind IDOR (insecure direct object reference) and broken-access-control bugs.

topics.label: Password Hashing
topics.desc: Storing passwords as slow, one-way hashes using bcrypt, argon2, scrypt, or PBKDF2, tuned to be expensive so stolen databases resist brute-force cracking.

topics.label: Salting & Peppering
topics.desc: Adding a unique random salt (and optional secret pepper) per password so identical passwords hash differently, defeating precomputed rainbow-table attacks.

topics.label: Hashing vs Encryption
topics.desc: Distinguishing one-way hashing (irreversible, for passwords and integrity) from reversible encryption (for data you must read back), a frequently confused choice.

topics.label: Symmetric vs Asymmetric
topics.desc: Shared-key ciphers like AES (fast, for bulk data) versus public/private key pairs like RSA and ECC (for key exchange and signatures), usually combined in practice.

topics.label: HTTPS & TLS
topics.desc: Encrypting client-server traffic with TLS so data in transit cannot be read or tampered with, the non-negotiable baseline enforced by HSTS and modern browsers.

topics.label: Certificates & PKI
topics.desc: X.509 certificates issued by certificate authorities (and free via Let's Encrypt) that bind a public key to a domain, letting clients verify server identity in TLS.

topics.label: Encryption at Rest
topics.desc: Protecting stored data with disk/database encryption and KMS-managed keys (complementing TLS in transit), a standard compliance and defense-in-depth requirement.

topics.label: OWASP Top 10
topics.desc: The community-standard list of the most critical web application security risks, the canonical checklist every developer should map their app against.

topics.label: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
topics.desc: Injecting malicious JavaScript into pages so it runs in victims' browsers, prevented by output encoding, CSP, and framework auto-escaping rather than raw HTML insertion.

topics.label: Cross-Site Request Forgery
topics.desc: Tricking a logged-in user's browser into firing unintended state-changing requests, defended with anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies.

topics.label: SQL Injection
topics.desc: Smuggling SQL through unsanitized input to read or destroy a database, eliminated by parameterized queries and ORMs instead of string-concatenated queries.

topics.label: Command & Code Injection
topics.desc: Untrusted input flowing into a shell, eval, or template that the system then executes, ranging from OS command injection to server-side template injection.

topics.label: Server-Side Request Forgery
topics.desc: Coercing the server into making attacker-chosen requests, often to reach internal services or cloud metadata endpoints, mitigated by allowlisting outbound URLs.

topics.label: Broken Access Control
topics.desc: The number-one OWASP risk where missing or flawed authorization lets users reach data or actions beyond their rights, including IDOR and privilege escalation.

topics.label: Clickjacking & Open Redirect
topics.desc: Framing your site to hijack clicks, and redirecting to attacker URLs for phishing, both blocked by frame-ancestors/X-Frame-Options and strict redirect allowlisting.

topics.label: CORS
topics.desc: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing headers that explicitly relax the same-origin policy for trusted origins, frequently misconfigured to a dangerous wildcard with credentials.

topics.label: Content Security Policy
topics.desc: A response header whitelisting allowed script, style, and resource sources, a strong second line of defense that limits the damage of any XSS that slips through.

topics.label: Security Headers
topics.desc: Hardening responses with HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, and Referrer-Policy, conveniently set in Node via the Helmet middleware.

topics.label: Input Validation & Sanitization
topics.desc: Rejecting or cleaning untrusted input at the boundary with allowlist schemas (Zod, Joi) and sanitizers (DOMPurify), the root defense behind most injection classes.

topics.label: Secrets Management
topics.desc: Keeping API keys and credentials out of source code using environment variables (.env, gitignored) and vaults like HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager.

topics.label: Rate Limiting
topics.desc: Throttling requests and login attempts with quotas, exponential backoff, and CAPTCHAs to stop brute-forcing, credential stuffing, and denial-of-service abuse.

topics.label: Dependency & Supply-Chain Security
topics.desc: Auditing third-party packages for known vulnerabilities and tampering using npm audit, Dependabot, Snyk, and lockfiles, since most app code is borrowed.

topics.label: Secure by Default
topics.desc: Designing systems so the safe choice is the automatic one—deny-by-default access, HTTPS everywhere, least privilege—rather than relying on developers to opt in.
